## COLD
A: Three days after the Republican Party lost both chambers of Congress, the White House has a new chief of staff. He's the architect of the administration's immigration enforcement.

## TITLE
A: From Void News, this is On Air. It's Saturday, November seventh.
A: Today: Stephen Miller takes the chief of staff's office on Monday, and the reaction splits along party lines before he's sat down. Then overnight, thirty-six Russian ballistic missiles over Ukraine, and a bridge in Kyiv closed in both directions.

## LEAD | Miller Takes the West Wing
A: Let's start with what the president actually announced.
B: On Friday, President Donald Trump announced that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. It takes effect on Monday, November ninth. Miller's the deputy chief of staff right now. On Friday evening he was at Mar-a-Lago, and he pledged loyalty to the president.
A: And Susie Wiles? She'd been there since the start of this term.
B: She had, and she was the first woman to hold the post. Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday night. According to the president's announcement, she's moving to his political operation.
A: So this lands three days after the midterms. How bad were they for the party?
B: Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress. They dropped at least forty-four House seats and seven Senate seats. And there's a number that sits behind this appointment: a Fox News exit survey found fifty-eight percent of voters believed federal immigration enforcement had gone too far. Miller is the person most identified with that enforcement.
A: Remind us what he's actually done on immigration.
B: He's forty-one, and he's been a central architect of the administration's immigration actions across both terms. That's the zero-tolerance border policy of twenty eighteen, the travel restrictions on several Muslim-majority nations, and an executive push directing Immigration and Customs Enforcement to arrest three thousand people a day. Congress backed that enforcement with about one hundred seventy billion dollars under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, passed in July of last year.
A: So how's the appointment landing?
B: Sharply, and along party lines. Pete Hegseth and the former congressman Matt Gaetz publicly backed the move. The incoming House majority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, called Miller a dangerous extremist with American blood on his hands, and urged the president to reverse the appointment. And it's not only Democrats: Republican critics and business sectors expressed concern about Miller's focus on hardline enforcement after Tuesday's results.
A: That's the reaction. What about the coverage? Where do the outlets differ?
B: They differ on what the story is. The Daily Beast and CNN emphasise internal West Wing infighting and factional tensions, and they liken the environment to the administration's early turmoil. The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller focus on the official resignation statements and on praise from administration figures. The Daily Beast also reported behind-the-scenes lobbying calls by Katie Miller, urging Trump allies to back her husband for the post. The Associated Press and RTE didn't address that account. The Washington Post framed the appointment around pushback from industries facing enforcement pressure. And Newsweek and The Hill led with Miller's remarks at Mar-a-Lago, declaring the Republican Party stronger than ever.
A: And where do those outlets sit on the roster?
B: Of the sixty outlets Void placed on this story, twenty-four sit left of centre, twenty at the centre and sixteen right of it.

## SECOND | Kyiv Under Fire Before Talks
B: In Kyiv, what came down overnight?
A: Russian forces launched thirty-six ballistic missiles and one hundred seventy-two strike drones across twelve Ukrainian regions. Kyiv was the heaviest target. At least nine people were injured across the country, including a child, and a kindergarten in the Solomianskyi district was partially destroyed.
B: And the bridge?
A: Explosions hit the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, a span of about eight hundred and sixteen metres. The city closed it to traffic in both directions. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, says municipal workers have started repairs, and water pressure and heating in the capital were partially restored. Elsewhere, three consecutive strikes hit a Naftogaz oil and gas facility in central Ukraine and set off a large fire. The company's acting chairman, Serhiy Fedorenko, says the fire was contained with no staff casualties.
B: What does Russia say it was aiming at?
A: The Russian Ministry of Defense confirmed the strikes. It says the operation targeted Ukraine's military-industrial production, energy installations and transport networks. And the timing matters: the assault came just before scheduled trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, with delegations from Russia, Ukraine and the United States, aimed at ending the war.
B: So how does the coverage split, and where do the outlets sit?
A: Ukrainian outlets and officials detailed civilian casualties and damage to homes, kindergartens and municipal utilities. Russian state coverage focused exclusively on military and industrial targets, including the Meridian missile plant and the Tripolskaya thermal power station. Local Ukrainian reports tracked damage in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro, while the international wires centred on the capital and the Abu Dhabi talks. Of the twenty-one outlets Void placed on this story, six sit left of centre, thirteen at the centre and two right of it.

## DESK
A: The rest of the desk.
A: In Krakow, five people were killed and more than a dozen injured on Saturday afternoon. A gunman drove a car into the Main Market Square and fired at random. Police shot and arrested him.
B: President Trump says he'll soon decide whether to launch new strikes against Iran or pursue a deal to end the eight-month conflict. Oil traded near ninety dollars a barrel.
A: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth faces an impeachment vote in the House next week, after Representative Thomas Massie introduced articles against him. The president says he keeps his confidence in Hegseth.
B: In Israel, sixty-seven members of parliament recommended the opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government, against forty-six for Benjamin Netanyahu. President Isaac Herzog announces the mandate on Sunday.
A: Abdul El-Sayed won the Senate race in Michigan, fifty-two percent to forty-six, over the Republican Mike Rogers. He becomes the first Muslim elected to the chamber.
B: Several incoming Democratic senators say they won't support Chuck Schumer for majority leader. Schumer states he has sufficient votes within his caucus to retain his leadership position.

## CLOSE
A: That's On Air from Void News. On Monday, Stephen Miller walks into the chief of staff's office; the Congress that meets him in January is one his party no longer controls. Every source, every story, at Void News.
